To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
Most (84%) women report having had breast or cervical screening, but a small proportion (3%) report never having had screening.

most (84%) eligible UK women report having had breast and cervical screening but 3% of those aged 40-64 years report never having had screening; inequalities exist in the uptake of screening, which are different for breast and cervical screening; indicators of wealth are important for breast screening, whereas ethnicity is important for cervical screening; and, the routine collection within general practices of additional sociodemography information would aid monitoring and policies to correct inequalities.

most (84%) eligible British women report having had mammography and cervical screening; some inequalities exist in the use of screening, but they are small and differ by screening type (wealth is important for mammography, ethnicity for cervical screening); and the routine collection within general practices of additional sociodemographics would help to monitor inequalities and inform policies to improve coverage.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the use of mammography and cervical smears.
the use of breast and cervix screening in the UK and how this varies according to the social characteristics of the population.
the extent to which women’s use of breast and cervix screening is related to their sociodemographic characteristics and the implications for monitoring and improving screening.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
there is no evidence to suggest that women from ethnic minority groups are any less likely than their white counterparts to have ever had a cervical screen.
the majority of women in the UK are screened regularly for both breast and cervical cancers.
there is no conclusive evidence of inequalities in breast screening uptake, and that there is some evidence of inequalities in cervical screening uptake.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the most significant inequalities were found in the uptake of cervical screening and were largely explained by ethnicity, whereas for breast screening, the most significant inequalities in uptake were explained by housing tenure and car ownership.
there are inequalities in the uptake of breast and cervical cancer screening, which are not well understood.
we have demonstrated the value of using the National Statistics Omnibuses Survey for research into health behaviours.
The main takeaway from our work is that
there are still significant inequalities in screening uptake, particularly for cervical screening.

the routine collection within general practices of additional sociodemographics (eg, ethnicity, housing tenure, education) would aid monitoring of screening coverage and inform policy to address inequalities in uptake of screening.
there are inequalities in reported use of screening.
